title: Hatikvah

segments.voice: Yesterday, each link, and your line: receives, and passes on. Today, a song about what gets handed on when there's little else to hold.

A valley full of bones, very dry. That's the scene the prophet Ezekiel describes. In his vision, God tells him the bones are the whole house of Israel, and tells him what the people are saying, a sentence of despair. Our bones are dried up, they say, and "our hope is lost". In Hebrew: avdah tikvatenu. Keep that phrase in your ear. Long after Ezekiel, a poem answered it almost word for word. The poem became a song, the song became a national anthem, and its name, a single Hebrew word, is today's word.
screen: `A VALLEY OF DRY BONES.` → `OUR HOPE IS LOST.` → `A POEM ANSWERS BACK.`

segments.voice: Hatikvah. Ha means the, and tikvah means hope: the hope. It's Israel's national anthem, and it's often sung at Jewish gatherings in other countries too. The words are short. In plain English, roughly: as long as, deep in the heart, a Jewish soul still yearns, and an eye still looks forward to the east, toward Zion, our hope is not yet lost, the hope of two thousand years: to be a free people in our land, the land of Zion and Jerusalem. Now listen for Ezekiel. The people said avdah tikvatenu, our hope is lost. The anthem sings od lo avdah tikvatenu, our hope is not yet lost. Two small words, od lo, not yet, turn despair around. Ezekiel's vision does the same. Before those words are even quoted, the bones have come together and breath has entered them, and right after, God promises to open the graves and bring the people home to the land of Israel. Notice what kind of hope the anthem sings. Not a victory song about something already won, but a hope still held, with the heart and the eyes, facing a direction. The year met this kind of hope before: in prayers that faced Jerusalem, in exile after exile, in people who kept saying next year. People hear the anthem differently, too. Israel has citizens who aren't Jewish, and some have said a song about a Jewish soul doesn't speak for them; that conversation is part of Israel's life. But the word at the song's center is one the Bible and the anthem share.
screen: `HA, THE. TIKVAH, HOPE.` · `A SOUL YEARNS, AN EYE LOOKS TO ZION.` · `OUR HOPE IS NOT YET LOST.` · `A HOPE STILL HELD, NOT A VICTORY SONG.` · then, large: `THE HOPE.`

segments.voice: Find one hope you've carried for a while: not a wish for a thing, but a hope for a person, a place, a change that hasn't come yet, said in a few plain words. Then put the anthem's two small words in front of it: not yet. If you pray, bring that hope before God in your own words; if you don't, simply keep it company, still unfinished, still held.
Hatikvah. The hope: Israel's anthem, which answers the dry bones' our hope is lost with our hope is not yet lost. Today's word.
Your line: the hope. Two small words in front of it: od lo, not yet. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hatikvah is sung at state ceremonies in Israel and at Jewish community events, school graduations and gatherings in other countries, often with the audience standing.

chat.says: Why is Israel's anthem called The Hope? Aren't anthems usually about winning?
options: Hatikvah means the hope; it sings that our hope is not yet lost.
It's named for a victory song from the day the state began.
It's called that because Ezekiel's bones sing it in the Bible.
chat.meaning: Ha means the and tikvah means hope. The anthem answers Ezekiel's our hope is lost with not yet lost: a hope still held.

Ezekiel.meaning: a prophet who saw a vision of a valley of dry bones

avdah tikvatenu.meaning: Hebrew: our hope is lost, the people's words in Ezekiel

od lo.meaning: Hebrew: not yet, the anthem's answer to despair

Zion.meaning: a name for Jerusalem and the land, the anthem's direction

sources.ref: Hatikvah, the words of Israel's national anthem (from a poem by Naftali Herz Imber)

notes: Claims rule: 'two thousand years' is said only as part of the anthem's own words (bat shnot alpayim). No dates for the poem or for the anthem's adoption are given; the poet is named only in the sources line, not the voice.
Anthem words given as a paraphrase in plain English, not a quotation. Please confirm the paraphrase of the current text.

Ezekiel 37:11 quoted only as 'our hope is lost' (JPS 1917); the rest of the verse paraphrased. The link between the anthem's 'od lo avdah tikvatenu' and Ezekiel's 'avdah tikvatenu' is stated as a word-for-word echo, not as the poet's stated intention. Please confirm.
Fairness: the voice notes that some of Israel's non-Jewish citizens have said the anthem doesn't speak for them. Please confirm this framing is fair and appropriate here.
'Sung at Jewish gatherings in other countries too' and howItsDone 'often with the audience standing': please confirm.
'The year has met this kind of hope before' refers back to day 997 (next year in Jerusalem) and the exile days in Block D.

Editor: fixed the order of Ezekiel 37 (the bones come together and receive breath in verses 7–10, before the despairing words of verse 11; the promise of verses 12–14 follows), and made clear the speakers are the house of Israel; replaced the illogical 'that's why the year has kept running into it'; softened 'sung at Jewish gatherings' to 'often sung'.

Audit: Ezekiel 37:11 has God report what the house of Israel is saying ('behold, they say'); God does not give them the words, and the revived bones are not the speakers.
